content: The Loblolly Pine, scientifically known as Pinus taeda, is one of several pine species native to the southeastern United States. It is a prominent tree species in this region, capable of reaching heights of 30 to 35 meters (100 to 115 feet) under normal conditions. Exceptional specimens, however, can grow as tall as 45 meters (150 feet), making it the tallest among the southern pines. The needles of the Loblolly Pine are arranged in bundles of three. These needles are sometimes twisted and measure between 12 and 22 centimeters (5 to 9 inches) in length. This length is considered intermediate among southern pines, being shorter than the needles of the Longleaf Pine or Slash Pine but longer than those of the Shortleaf Pine and Spruce Pine. The cones of the Loblolly Pine are 7 to 13 centimeters (3 to 5 inches) wide, with each scale bearing a sharp spine measuring 3 to 6 millimeters. The name Loblolly refers to a low, wet area, but these trees are not restricted to such habitats. Historically, the tree has been known by other names, though these are now rarely used. Oldfield Pine reflects its role as an early colonizer of abandoned fields. Bull Pine refers to its large size, a name also applied to other large yellow pines. Rosemary Pine is a reference to its distinctive fragrance, which is more reminiscent of gin than rosemary and sets it apart from other southern pines. With the advent of fire control practices, Loblolly Pines have become dominant in areas of the Deep South that were once more heavily populated by Longleaf Pines and, in Florida, Slash Pines. The Loblolly Pine is known for its rapid growth rate, even among the generally fast-growing southern pines. Its yellowish, resinous wood is highly valued for lumber and is also used in the production of pulp fibers. The tree is commercially cultivated in extensive plantations, often alongside Slash Pine. Although the Loblolly Pine primarily grows in the Deep South, its range extends northward along the mid-Atlantic coast to southern New Jersey, westward to the southeastern and southwestern corners of Kentucky, and as far west as the southeastern corner of Oklahoma and central Texas. Notably, it is the pine species found in the Lost Pines area near Bastrop, Texas, and in McKinney Roughs along the Texas Colorado River. These populations are isolated, growing on acidic sandy soils surrounded by alkaline clays, which are unsuitable for pine growth. One famous Loblolly Pine was the Eisenhower Tree, located on the 17th hole of Augusta National Golf Club. President Dwight D. Eisenhower, a member of the club, frequently hit this tree during his golf games. In 1956, he proposed at a club meeting that the tree be cut down. To avoid offending the President, the club's chairman, Clifford Roberts, adjourned the meeting immediately rather than outright rejecting the request.
